---
title: Connectors
description: How a connector brings records from another service into Marfa, and what the instance keeps so it can stop and resume safely.
---

Much of what a person keeps starts somewhere else: events in Google Calendar, issues on GitHub, highlights in Readwise. A **connector** is a program outside the server that **registers with the instance**, most often to read such a service, its vendor, and write what it finds as items. It can also carry changes made in Marfa back to the vendor.

The registration is what makes a program a connector. An app or a script that reads and writes with a key, or through a sign-in, but never registers isn't one, and needs nothing on this page.

A Todoist connector, for example, runs where you choose and reaches the instance with a key of its own. The instance keeps what the connector needs to resume, and Todoist can also post webhooks to an inbound endpoint on the instance.

<ConnectorParts />

## A program you run

The server never runs a connector or calls a vendor. A connector is an ordinary program you run wherever suits you, on a schedule or all the time, and it uses the same API as any app. That keeps the server small, and your vendor credentials out of it.

**A connector registers under a key made for it alone**, and a key holds one registration. An app's sign-in can't register one. [Build a connector](/build/connector#make-its-key-and-run-it) makes the key through the server's private socket.

The key's [source](/build/items-and-types#where-an-item-came-from) labels everything the connector writes. It names the system the records come from, such as `github`, never an account or the route they took. With each record's `source_id`, its ID at the vendor, the source lets the connector update a record rather than write it twice. An account goes into `source_id` only for what it owns, such as a calendar.

A connector also gives its source a **name** and an optional **mark**, so an app shows "GitHub" with its logo rather than the code. It sets only what the source lacks, so a name the owner chose stays, as [Name the source](/build/connector-pull#name-the-source) shows.

What a connector brings in belongs in the [feed](/build/items-and-types#library-and-feed). A connector names `feed` on each write, or its key makes `feed` its default; otherwise its records land in the library.

## Links between records

A connector links what it writes with the [edge type](/build/edges#edge-types) that says what each link means: a GitHub comment `comments-on` its issue, a notification is `about` the pull request it concerns, and a Readwise highlight is an `excerpt-of` its book. Its key needs write on each edge type it writes.

When a connector stops writing an edge type, it lists it as **retired**, and the kit removes the edges of that type it wrote itself, never one a person drew. The key keeps write on that edge type to do it.

## Edits a connector puts back

A connector that takes no edits back for a type, such as an RSS entry, puts back any edit a person makes there on its next run. **It says so in its registration**, and the type's items read `read_only: true`, so an app can show them locked. Marfa refuses no write for it. [Pull from a vendor](/build/connector-pull#declare-the-types-you-dont-carry-back) shows how.

## What the instance keeps for a connector

A connector can stop, restart or move to another computer without losing its place, because the instance keeps what it needs:

| What | What it's for |
| --- | --- |
| A registration | Names the connector and the types it holds read only, and shows its last heartbeat and how its recent runs went. |
| A state document | A JSON object the connector resumes from, such as the vendor's sync token. |
| Current problems | Messages about unresolved trouble, such as a record the vendor refused, until the connector clears them. |
| Agreements | One record per item of what the connector and the vendor last agreed about it, so a two-way connector can tell a change a person made from its own. |
| A hold | Lets one process at a time write, so two copies started by mistake don't overwrite each other. |

The state document, current problems and agreements belong to the key's **source**, not to one key. Replace a connector's key with one under the same source, and the connector picks up where it stopped. Revoking a key leaves its registration and its runs in place.

## Webhooks from the vendor

Many vendors post a webhook when something changes, so a connector can act at once. The instance can give a connector an **inbound endpoint**, a private address the vendor posts to.

The instance stores each delivery as it arrived, and **the connector does the rest**: it reads the deliveries, checks each came from the vendor, and marks them handled. [Receive vendor webhooks](/build/connector-webhooks) shows how.

## Building one

[Build a connector](/build/connector) walks through one from a template, and [Make a connector follow changes](/build/connector-follow-changes) teaches it to archive what the vendor drops and report a failed run. The six connectors Marfa ships, listed in the [Catalog](/catalog/connectors), are working examples in [withmarfa/marfa-connectors](https://github.com/withmarfa/marfa-connectors), and [Run a connector](/use/connect-a-service) runs any of them.

The rules behind this page are in the [connectors](https://github.com/withmarfa/marfa/blob/main/conformance/spec/connectors.md) and [inbound webhooks](https://github.com/withmarfa/marfa/blob/main/conformance/spec/inbound-webhooks.md) chapters of the contract.
